content: Alkaline tide is a physiological phenomenon that occurs after the consumption of a meal. During this process, the stomach releases hydrochloric acid (HCl) into its lumen to aid in digestion. This release of acid is accompanied by a temporary increase in the pH of the blood, making it more alkaline. The underlying mechanism involves the activity of gastric parietal cells, which are responsible for producing HCl. These cells extract chloride (Cl⁻) ions, carbon dioxide (CO₂), water (H₂O), and sodium (Na⁺) ions from the blood plasma. Within the parietal cells, CO₂ and H₂O are converted into carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. Carbonic acid then dissociates into hydrogen ions (H⁺) and bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻). The hydrogen ions are secreted into the stomach lumen, combining with chloride ions to form HCl. To maintain electrical neutrality in the plasma, the bicarbonate ions generated during this process are transported back into the bloodstream. This results in the venous blood leaving the stomach being more alkaline compared to the arterial blood entering it. The temporary rise in blood pH due to the increased bicarbonate concentration is referred to as the alkaline tide. In children, this shift in pH can sometimes lead to complications associated with the alkaline tide, as their physiological systems may be more sensitive to such changes.
